Hi Frédéric,

One would not want to pass a right-hand-side only variable to $calculate. Rather than using `$getVarNames()` (which includes right-hand-side only variables in its output), please use `$getNodeNames()` and `$getDependencies()` to determine nodes for calculation. By default, those methods will not include right-hand-side only nodes in their output.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
This seems to be an issue for folks in the Bayesian class I'm teaching.

For the sake of helping the nimble folks track down the internal error, here's an example of what caused it.
One student had this error after running:
prepnim <- nimbleModel(code = CJS_sex_year, constants = constants, dat = data_list,
                       inits = inits, calculate = T)

and then trying to do:

mcmc_out <- nimbleMCMC(
  code = CJS_sex_year,
  constants = constants,
  data = data_list,
  inits = inits,
  monitors = params,
  niter = 6000,
  nburnin = 3000,
  nchains = 3,
  thin = 1,
  samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE
)

It seems that sometimes the two forms of running the model clash somehow, even if everything in R is cleared but R is not restarted. Restarting R seems to help.

messages.body_plain:
Hello All. I am estimating density using distance sampled line transect data. I have hundreds of observations of animal groups at 127 sites.  Because the detections are of groups with group-level traits that can influence detection (such as group size) i am using data augmentation to loop over each group.  I have augmented variables that includes distance, site, group size, and y - an indicator variable for whether the observations is real or an augment using code based on Kery and Royle 2016 (Chapter 9). I have several site-specific variables in the model for abundance at sites.  Despite fitting abundance models with 8 variables or more, the nimble model runs take no more than 2 hours and the results demonstrate good mixing.
I also want to explore the effects of site-specific variables, like tree cover, on detection.  This requires dynamic indexing because tree cover is site-specific and site is group-specific and unknown for all augmented groups. However, adding a single dynamically indexed variable to the linear model for log sigma - the scale parameter in the half normal detection function - results in models that are 10 times slower, requiring 20 hours or more to resolve. I do not get any errors and have confirmed that the model structure is consistent with the data structure.  The site specific covariate, tree cover, has been listed as a data argument in the nimble model, not a constant.
I can't discern why the model takes so much longer to run after adding the dynamically indexed variable to the model for sigma.  I have pasted the loop that contains the line with the offending site covariate, tree cover, to the model for sigma. Tree cover is the proportion of the site covered with trees with a mean of about 0.2 (range 0.07, 0.45) and has no missing values. Thanks in advance for any suggestions or advice you can offer or if you have an explanation for why this is resulting in such a dramatic decrease in efficiency.

for(i in 1:M){ # M is number of observed groups plus augments)
    groupsize[i] ~ dnegbin(pgroup, r) # size of groups
    z[i] ~ dbern(psi) # does the group exist
    d[i] ~ dunif(0,B) # distance (continuous) from the transect line with half-strip B
    site[i] ~ dcat(site.probs[1:nsites]) # site assignment based on pop distribution among sites
    sigma[i] <- exp(alpha0 + alpha1*log(groupsize[i]+1) + alpha2*treecover[site[i]])
    p[i] <- exp(-d[i]*d[i]/(2*sigma[i]*sigma[i])) #half normal detection fxn
    y[i] ~ dbern(p[i]*z[i]) # observation model
  }

messages.subject_clean: efficient generation of a distribution of Bayesian p-values
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I am trying to set up simulation code to generate a distribution of Bayesian p-values. The idea is for each of n simulated datasets, I will fit the model and calculate a Bayesian p-value using the observed data and posterior predictive replicated data.

I am trying to avoid compiling the model over and over again for each simulated dataset, so I am hoping to repeatedly use the same compiled model. Also as a note, I am adding simulated data to the model, rather than simulating data with the model, since I am trying to develop a workflow where the model can be the wrong data-generating process.

With the below code, in the second iteration of the n_datasets loop, I am getting the following error in the compileNimble(mcmc, project = compiled_model) part of the fit_model() function.
Error in nimbleProject$instantiateCmodelValues(thisObj, dll) : Trying to instantiate a modelValues type that the project has no record of. Try setting option resetFunctions = TRUE in compileNimble

It seems like the MCMC settings need to be reset somehow? And also, I'm wondering if there are any general tips on setting this up to be the most efficient?

Thanks so much!
Abby Keller

The general code set-up is like this:

# create model instance and compile
model <- nimbleModel(model_code, constants = constants)
compiled_model <- compileNimble(model)

for (i in 1:n_datasets) {

  # add simulated data to compiled model
  compiled_model$y <- simulate_data(params)

  # fit model
  samples <- fit_model(model, compiled_model, niter, nburnin, thin)

  # calculate p values
  p_values[i, "deviance"] <- mean(samples[, "D_rep_total"] > samples[, "D_obs_total"])
  p_values[i, "chi_sq"] <- mean(samples[, "chi_rep_total"] > samples[, "chi_obs_total"])
}

Where fit_model() looks like this:

fit_model <- function(model, compiled_model, niter, nburnin, thin) {

  # function for generating initial values
  inits <- function(y) list(psi = runif(1, 0, 1), p = runif(1, 0, 1), z = pmin(rowSums(y), 1))

  # add initial values
  compiled_model$setInits(inits(compiled_model$y))

  # configure MCMC
  mcmc_conf <- configureMCMC(model,
                             monitors = c("psi", "p", "z", "D_obs_total", "D_rep_total",
                                                      "chi_obs_total", "chi_rep_total"))

  # build and compile MCMC
  mcmc <- buildMCMC(mcmc_conf)
  compiled_mcmc <- compileNimble(mcmc, project = compiled_model)

  # generate posterior samples
  samples <- runMCMC(compiled_mcmc, niter = niter, nburnin = nburnin, thin = thin)

  return(samples)
}

messages.subject_clean: DA distance sampling model with dynamically indexed site variable slows model run
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

As a prefacing note to make sure we are on the same page, I assume that you are setting `d`, `site`, `groupsize`, via the `data` argument with fixed (known) values for the observed groups and NA values for the augmented groups. In this case, nimble should impute values for the augmented groups for those variables.

Also, is it the case that M is the maximum possible number of groups and then you are some imputing groups that "exist" but are not observed. And then the remaining groups don't actually exist?  So there will be groups that exist but are not observed, with y[i]=0 and z[i]=1 and then groups that don't exist, with y[i]=0 and z[i]=0?

In general, nimble's MCMC system tries to distinguish predictive nodes that have no data dependencies from nodes that have data dependencies.  The former can be sampled separately based on their prior distributions (using the current prior parameter values in that MCMC iteration), and when we sample the parameters, we avoid conditioning the MCMC updates on the predictive nodes (which generally will help improve MCMC mixing). If you had missing values in `y` then nimble should detect them and various of their parent nodes as predictive nodes. But if all the elements of `y` are known, then that means that there would not be any predictive nodes in the full model.

In the simpler model, nimble can treat `site[i]` for the augmented groups as a predictive node as no `y[i]` depends on it. But in the full model, those would not be predictive nodes because `y[i]` is data and depends on `site[i]`. So then the sampling for `site[i]` gets a lot more computationally intensive and as well the dependencies in the MCMC are more complicated and probably slow down mixing.

I think I'll need to see the full model code to say more, particularly in terms of seeing any potential solutions/work-arounds. And if you could provide real or simulated data to allow me to build the model and look at the MCMC configuration for the two cases, that would be helpful.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
hi David,

Thanks for providing your code off-list.

Here's what I am seeing:

1. When `alpha2*treecover[site[i]]` is not in the model, `site[i]` is sampled using a posterior predictive sampler, which just samples categorically (based on the current values in `site.probs`), which is presumably fast.
2. When `alpha2*treecover[site[i]]` is in the model, then the sampling for `site[i]` depends on `y[i]` and the MCMC needs to calculate 127 probabilities, one for each possible value `site[i]` could take. And it does this for the 990 unknown `site[i]` nodes. While calculating those 127 probabilities is straightforward, I think it is enough additional calculation (relative to the calculations involved in sampling all the other nodes in the model), that it slows down the time it takes to complete each iteration by a lot.
3. I don't think the presence of dynamic indexing itself is important here. The dynamic indexing only affects sampling of `alpha2`, which is a single node, and based on the model structure, I don't think it matters whether sampling `alpha2` involves any dynamic indexing or not, as regardless of that, all of the data values are dependencies of `alpha2`, so the full likelihood needs to be calculated in order to sample `alpha2`. In other situations, it can be the case that dynamic indexing can drastically increase the number of dependencies when sampling node(s) and drive up sampling time.
4. I wouldn't think that the difference in sampling the `site[i]` nodes would affect mixing of the other nodes. Can you confirm that 10x increase in time is primarily driven by pure sampling time and not by worse mixing of the nodes that appear in both the smaller and larger models? And is the mixing of the `site[i]` nodes or of `alpha2` in the larger model problematic? Basically I'd like to know what seems to cause the 10x slowdown - computation time or mixing, and if the latter, which nodes are the problematic ones?

Unfortunately, while your response to the above questions in (4) might give me some ideas, at the moment, I'm not seeing anything to suggest that would improve the situation.

-chris

In this case, nimble should impute values for the augmented groups for those variables.
>

So there will be groups that exist but are not observed, with y[i]=0 and z[i]=1 and then groups that don't exist, with y[i]=0 and z[i]=0?
>
> In general, nimble's MCMC system tries to distinguish predictive nodes that have no data dependencies from nodes that have data dependencies.  The former can be sampled separately based on their prior distributions (using the current prior parameter values in that MCMC iteration), and when we sample the parameters, we avoid conditioning the MCMC updates on the predictive nodes (which generally will help improve MCMC mixing). If you had missing values in `y` then nimble should detect them and various of their parent nodes as predictive nodes. But if all the elements of `y` are known, then that means that there would not be any predictive nodes in the full model.
>
> In the simpler model, nimble can treat `site[i]` for the augmented groups as a predictive node as no `y[i]` depends on it. But in the full model, those would not be predictive nodes because `y[i]` is data and depends on `site[i]`. So then the sampling for `site[i]` gets a lot more computationally intensive and as well the dependencies in the MCMC are more complicated and probably slow down mixing.
>
> I think I'll need to see the full model code to say more, particularly in terms of seeing any potential solutions/work-arounds. And if you could provide real or simulated data to allow me to build the model and look at the MCMC configuration for the two cases, that would be helpful.

I think this is a case where you should be able to reuse a single compiled MCMC and not need to keep rebuilding and compiling the MCMC.

In the later datasets (after all the usual steps for the first dataset) I think you should be able to put the new `y` values into the compiled model (as you are doing), and then rerun the MCMC using the existing compiled MCMC via `runMCMC`. Let us know if that doesn't work.

As a sidenote, if you were not able to reuse the compiled MCMC, this might be a situation in which using the `resetFunctions` argument to `compileNimble` might be relevant, but I think that is moot, given my suggestion above.

-chris

I am encountering a similar issue in a distance sampling model I am using that includes both step() and pnorm() functions. I have written wrapper nimbleFunctions to exclude them from derivative tracking but then encounter this error:
"In C++, a model node is being included in derivatives that does not support them.

          To skip this error handling entirely (and allow possible malformed code to be used),
          set `nimbleOptions(unsupportedDerivativeHandling='ignore')`."

In the manual: "functions and distributions that are not supported can still be used in a model, as long as no algorithm tries to take derivatives with respect to node(s) that is (are) not supported", and I don't believe I am since, I think, the derivatives are taken on the continuous nodes that are upstream. I am confused as to why this error hasn't already appeared in this thread because it seems like the same underlying issue. My aim is to get the HMC sampler for the "p_eps_sd" hyperparameter in the toy-model code because this mixes very slowly with the default sampler.

I have 3 questions:
1) why does the model compile fine when there is no wrapper for the step() function but does not compile without a wrapper for the pnorm() function even though in the manual, neither is supported for AD?
2) can anyone comment on the validity of the model given that other users seem to have avoided this issue by wrapping unsupported function for AD in nimbleFunctions?
3) how is my situation different from the above / why did this error message not come up in this thread previously?

Best,
Simon

messages.subject_clean: Error requiring simulation function for user-defined distribution
messages.body_plain:
Brook, this is a good question.  The automatic registration of distributions should have handled this, but you're correct that it doesn't.

When a custom-written distribution is "registered" in nimble (allowing it to be used in a model), nimble checks for the density function (the d-function), and also looks for the random generation function (the r-function).  If it doesn't find the random generation function, then it creates one for you (which won't operate correctly, but it's a placeholder), and then registers them for use.

When you jump right into calling nimbleMCMC, this registration does take place, but something is going awry with the generation of (or more possible, the location of) the random generation function.  This is something we'll have to look into.

In the meantime, just manually registering your dmyexp distribution (before calling nimbleMCMC) will take care of this for you:

registerDistributions('dmyexp')

Let me know if this works ok for you.

Cheers!
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Yes, this is quite doable, without too much effort.

>From what you sent, it looks like you're attempting to generate samples for "y", is that correct?  And, that y is discrete-valued?  If so, then you'll need to register your distribution as being discrete, as shown below.

Also, make sure to *not* name the argument to your distribution as "x".  In the custom distribution definition, that name "x" is reserved for the variate which is following the distribution.  Here, below, I'm calling the single argument "arg"

registerDistributions(
    list(dmydist = list(
             BUGSdist = 'df(arg)',
             discrete = TRUE    ## necessary if distribution is discrete-valued
         ))
)

Also, is there any data in your model?  If not, then it would actually use a posterior predictive sampler, which would try to find the random generation r-function.  We can work around that if there's no data, but it would make a bit of a difference.

If you're able to provide the code you tried - including the model code itself, and your nimbleFunction definition of df() - then it won't be too much trouble to get it working.

Cheers,
Daniel

What you did works fine, and below is another approach which felt more natural to me - no need to introduce the Bernoulli distribution, or the "one" data.  Also, this no longer requires your function to be scaled down to attain values between 0 and 1.  Any (strictly non-negative, proportional) function will be fine.

Also, there was not even a possibility of "registration" of the distribution in your example, since it wasn't a "custom distribution", but rather a custom (deterministic) function.  Below, I actually use a custom *distribution*, called dfun, which gets automatically registered at the time of model building.

There's just a few comments in the code, but feel free to ask questions if anything is unclear.

Cheers!
Daniel

library(nimble)

## changed name to 'dfun' to avoid conflict with R's rf() function
dfun <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(x = double(0), log = integer(0, default = 0)) {
        returnType(double(0))
        pdf <- -8 * x * (x-1)
        ####pdf <- pdf / 2      # pdf(x) <= 1 for all x  --- no longer necessary
        if(log) return(log(pdf))
        else return(pdf)
    })

code <- nimbleCode({
    x ~ dfun()
})

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, inits = list(x = 0.5))

conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)
conf$replaceSampler('x', 'RW')    ## need to replace the default predictive sampler with a RW sampler

Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)

Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

mcmc.out <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, 100000)

I have written a hierarchical model with 4 levels of hierarchy: population<-individual animal<-individual year for that animal<-seasons within that year.  As would be expected, some animals are only recorded in a single year and/or don't have records from every season within a year.

The for loops to generate the priors are all written with indicator variables to generate a "ragged" output that only generates a prior if that animal existed that year and season. I use $getNodeNames and $getParents to define my monitors and it correctly identifies the data shape.

However, when I get the posteriors, everything has been squared off and I have posteriors that are all zero filling in what would be the holes in matrices and arrays (I did have to define my initial values with these "ghost values" because I am unaware of a way to define my inital values with uneven structure).

The outputs and estimates of the hyperparameters seem reasonable given my knowledge of the system being modeled and a subjective look at the different levels of the hierarchy feeding into each other. I have two questions. The first and most important is, do these values somehow skew my estimates? And second, how do I prevent them from being extracted? They are not included in my monitors and balloon my output, and provide no value to interpretation.

John

Hi John,
Thanks for the question. Monitoring of MCMC output is done on the basis of variables, not nodes. Hence, for better or worse, when a variable is involved in an entry for monitors, you will get the entire variable. The contents of elements that aren't used in the model can be ignored. One way to manage output size is to use monitors2 and thin2 with thin2 > thin to record fewer samples of large variables. But you will still get all elements of the variable (not ragged) in the output.
HTH
Perry

This reply is only looking at nimble software mechanics, not whether the math you're trying to do is correct.

For nimIntegrate(f, a, b, param), according to help(nimIntegrate), f must be a function (nimbleFunction) that accepts a vector first argument and returns a corresponding vector as output. (It also takes a vector second argument, theta as you have it.) In your first example, it looks like your innerFunc satisfies this protocol. Vector x is input and the result of the calculations you've made will be to return a vector output. However, it doesn't look like outerFunc satisfies this protocol. Vector y is input. But then it calls nimIntegrate and returns the value of that (first element of its return vector), which is a scalar. Hence outerFunc looks like it takes a vector input and returns a scalar, so it does not follow the protocol to be able to called within nimIntegrate. I am wondering if you need to write a for loop to iterate over values of y and call nimIntegrate of innerFunc for each value of y. I'm not following because y is not used at all in outerFunc. Nevertheless I hope this points you in the right direction.

It does seem that if you repeatedly call innerFunc, you will be repeatedly integrating over parts of the same thing, hence computationally it seems possible that you'd be better off writing this manually (including by a discretization method) rather than using nimIntegrate, in order to avoid redundant computations. But I am not sure.

HTH
Perry

messages.subject: Re: modeling with imputed data
messages.body_plain:
Brook, you have the right idea here, the only difference is for imputed nodes, you only need to prescribe their prior distribution using the dxxx() function, or using your notation from above:

x ~ f(theta)

But, then do *not* assign "x" as data.  You may wish to provide a valid initial value for x, however.  The MCMC will then identify these "predictive", or "imputed" stochastic nodes, and will impute values for them during the course of MCMC sampling.  This approach can be done using built-in distributions, such as the "dnorm" distribution as in your script.  Or, it can also work with "custom written" distributions, which you may yourself implement as nimbleFunctions.  If that's your goal, we can discuss how to do that.

Another question - is your goal to have "mu" and "sigma" be inferred from data?  That's the suggestion, when they have prior distributions.  However, when you provide values for "Mu" and "Sigma" as constants, it fixes their values.  I guess I'm confused if there are multiple "mu" and "Mu" terms, and same for "sigma" and "Sigma" in your script.

It also occurs to me that you most likely want to infer "mu" and "sigma" from some actual data values for x, and then impute new values.  I've modified your script to instead have 100 *data* values called "x" (generated from a normal(mu=3, sigma=2) distribution), which will inform the inferences for "mu" and "sigma".  Then, also impute 100 new values, into a new variable called xp.  I also changed all the "Mu" and "Sigma" in the model to be lowercase.

See the modified code below.

Cheers,
Daniel

library(nimble)

code <- nimbleCode({

    # infer (mu,sigma) from x
    for (i in 1:n) {
        x[i] ~ dnorm(mean=mu,sd=sigma)
    }

    # augment unobserved x with samples
    for (i in 1:n) {
        xp[i] ~ dnorm(mean=mu,sd=sigma)
    }

    # priors
    mu ~ dunif(-10,10)
    sigma ~ dunif(0,10)
})

Mu <- 0
Sigma <- 1

n <- 100
x <- rnorm(n, 3, 2)

MCMC_chains <- 1
MCMC_iterations <- 1000

constants <- list(n=n)   #####,Mu=Mu,Sigma=Sigma)
data <- list(x=x)
initial_values <- list(mu=Mu,sigma=Sigma, xp = rep(0,n))    ## added initial values for xp

mcmc.out <- nimbleMCMC(code=code,
                       constants=constants,
                       data=data,
                       inits=initial_values,
                       nchains=MCMC_chains,
                       niter=MCMC_iterations,
                       summary=TRUE,
                       monitors=c("mu","sigma", "xp"))     ## added a monitor for x

Are you able to install nimble from a developmental branch?  You can do so using the code below:

remove.packages('nimble')
library(remotes)
remotes::install_github('nimble-dev/nimble', ref = 'derived_quantities', subdir = 'packages/nimble')
library(nimble)

If that worked, then you can do exactly as you asked ("get a vector of log(L) values for each iteration of the MCMC"), using nimbleMCMC, as:

out <- nimbleMCMC(...., logProb = TRUE)

After that, the (summed) log(L) for the entire model will be available in:

out$derived$logProb

There is more fine grained control available also, if you only want the log(L) for certain sets of nodes.  If that's your goal, let me know, and we can discuss further.

Cheers,
Daniel

Hi Simon,
Apologies your question sat for a while. For context, since models and algorithms are separate, the warning given when compiling the model is the best that can be done (i.e. it can't actually error-trap based on an algorithm because it doesn't know how an algorithm will use the model). If your algorithm (an HMC in your case) were attempting to get derivatives for some model calculation that lacks derivative support, you would (should) get an error either when the algorithm is configured (ideally, if the error trapping does its job) or (worse) when it runs. You asked why this warning hadn't appeared in Russ' previous question on this thread. I would guess that's because he encountered a compilation error prior to when the warning would be issued. I'd think subsequently, he would have seen this warning, but perhaps didn't report it as it wasn't the topic of a question. He can confirm (if still following this).
To your other questions:
1. I think nimStep is actually supported (and may have mis-stated above), with 0 derivative everywhere (and I don't think well defined right at 0), so will have to check the manual and whether this makes sense. I think pnorm is not supported. I think the reason Russ encountered an issue with nimStep support involving using it in the larger expression in his code.
2. I'm hoping this is implicitly addressed.
3. I think I addressed this above.
HTH. Thanks for bringing the confusion to our attention.
Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sara,

Thanks for the question. The mcmc configuration exists only in R. After the MCMC has been built, the configuration has no further role. The control list is used for input but does not get updated or collect output in any way. Here are the steps you can take to see the internal variables of samplers.

nimbleOptions(buildInterfacesForCompiledNestedNimbleFunctions=TRUE)
# build, compile, and run your MCMC
# Then access internals like this
compiled_mcmc$samplerFunctions[[1]]$scale
# if, for example the first sampler is an adaptive random-walk Metropolis-Hastings, for which "scale" is the proposal std. dev.

To see what variables exist in each sampler, you would need to look at the source code in MCMC_samplers.R.

We refer to an object such as "compiled_mcmc" as an interface because it exists to access (interface to) a C++ object. We refer to an object such as "samplerFunctions[[1]]" as being nested since it lives only within compiled_mcmc. We do not by default build the interface for samplerFunctions[[1]] that allows you to do samplerFunctions[[1]]$scale because that creates a lot of overhead and is rarely needed. Hence the (verbosely named) nimbleOption will build any nested interfaces and you can thereby access the internal variables of any of the samplers.

HTH
Perry

Brook, I've modified your script to operate the way you were aiming for.  That's a good use of the dummy values for the x[] array, that's the right idea.  Also, there's no need for the nimbleRcalls, because you're only making calls to (otherwise compilable) functions dnorm and rnorm.  So that helped simplify things.

Daniel

library(nimble)

dNorm <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(x = double(), mean = double(), sd = double(), Mean = double(), SD = double(), log=integer(0, default = 0)) {
        ####y <- Rrnorm(mean=Mean,sd=SD)
        y <- rnorm(1, Mean, SD)
        ####pdf <- Rdnorm(y,mean=mean,sd=sd,log=log)
        lp <- dnorm(y, mean, sd, log = 1)
        returnType(double(0))
        return(lp)
    })

code <- nimbleCode({
    for(i in 1:n) {
        x[i] ~ dNorm(mean=mu, sd=sigma, Mean=Mu, SD=Sigma)
    }
    # priors
    mu ~ dunif(-10, 10)    ## dunif(-10*Mu, 10*Mu)
    sigma ~ dunif(0, 10*Sigma)

})

Mu <- 0
Sigma <- 1
n <- 10

x <- rep(0,n)

constants <- list(n=n, Mu=Mu, Sigma=Sigma)
data <- list(x=x)
inits <- list(mu=Mu, sigma=Sigma)

mcmc.out <- nimbleMCMC(code=code,
                       constants=constants,
                       data=data,

                       inits=inits,
                       niter=1000,
                       summary=TRUE,
                       monitors=c("mu","sigma"))

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am currently trying to model species richness using several environmental predictors, the most important among which is distance from a retreating glacier (a proxy of time since deglaciation). For this model, I am having serious difficulty getting convergence among my environmental covariates, even when they are centered and scaled. So much so that Rhat is "INF" in my MCMC summary output. I wondered if anyone had any quick fixes on this front, here is the code I am working with and can supply the data set if needed. This analysis is part of my Graduate Thesis. Thanks!

#### Model1B, Species Richness: Random effect for transect, distance and other covariates ####

Model1B_code <- nimbleCode({

  # Priors
  beta0 ~ dnorm(0, .00001)   #vague prior distribution for beta0
  beta1 ~ dnorm(0, .00001)   #vague prior distribution for beta1

  sd ~ dunif(0, 100)    #vague prior distribution for sd of epsilon
  ep.sig <- 1 / (sd*sd)      #convert sd to precision (nimble default is precision)

  sd2 ~ dunif(0, 100)    #vague prior distribution for sd of alpha
  t.sig <- 1 / (sd2*sd2)    #convert sd2 to precision (nimble default is precision)

  # Likelihood:
  for (i in 1:n){
    rich[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], ep.sig)
    mu[i] <- beta0 + beta1*dist[i] + beta2*twi[i] + beta3*tri[i] + beta4*gravfines[i] + alpha[t[i]]

    #For GOF/Bayesian p-value
    rich.sim[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], ep.sig)
    dev[i] <- -2*(-log(sd)-.5*log(6.283)- ((rich[i]-mu[i])^2)/(2*sd*sd))
    dev.sim[i] <- -2*(-log(sd)-.5*log(6.283)- ((rich.sim[i]-mu[i])^2)/(2*sd*sd))
  }
  for (j in 1:nSites){
    alpha[j] ~ dnorm(0, t.sig)
  }

  dev2 <- sum(dev[1:n])
  dev2.sim <- sum(dev.sim[1:n])

})

nSites = length(unique(model_data$transect))

# Bundle data
data.feed <- list(rich = as.numeric(model_data$richness),
                  n = as.numeric(length(model_data)),
                  dist = as.numeric(model_data$distance),
                  t = as.numeric(model_data$transect),
                  twi = as.numeric(model_data$twi),

messages.subject: sampler doesn't sample in parallel
messages.body_plain:
Hello All, Has anyone else encountered an issue where a node is sampled well on a single chain but the sampler sticks when running the model in parallel on multiple chains?  In my case, I started with a model that wasn't sampling a node on a single chain until I forced a slice sampler on that node.  However, when I switched to running in parallel, by wrapping my nimbleModel, compile, config, remove/add sampler, build, compile, run lines inside a function as recommended, the same nodes do not move beyond passed their initial values. Adjusting the sliceWidth control to start with a large initial width didn't help.  The parallelization is not effecting the other nodes in the model. I can also see from the trace plots that stuck nodes are accepting their random initial values.  Here is a snippet of the parallelization code where I think the problem must lie:
run_MCMC_allcode <- function(X, data, constants, code, monitors, niter, nburnin, thin){
  library(nimble)
  dmy_function<-nimbleFunction(...#custom function)
  assign(' dmy_function  ',  dmy_function  , envir = .GlobalEnv)
  inits <- X$inits
  # Build model
  model <- nimbleModel(code = code,
                       data = data,
                       constants = constants,
                       inits = inits)
  assign('rmy_function',  rmy_function  , envir = .GlobalEnv) # dummy random
  cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
  conf <- configureMCMC(cmodel, monitors = monitors)
  conf$removeSamplers(paste0("K[", 1:constants$S, "]")) # this is stuck node K: discrete scalars
  for(i in seq_len(constants$S)) {
    conf$addSampler(target = paste0("K[", i, "]"),
                    type   = "slice")
  }
  modbuild<- buildMCMC(conf)
  modc <- compileNimble(modbuild, project = model)
  seed <- X$seed
  results <- runMCMC(modc, niter = niter, nburnin = nburnin, thin = thin, setSeed = seed)
  return(list(results = results, seed = seed))
}

output <- parLapply(cl = cl, X = inputsList,
                      fun = run_MCMC_allcode,
                      data = data,
                      constants = constants,
                      code = code,
                      monitors = c("lambdaM","alpha","sigma","pbar",
                                    "M","K"),
                      niter = 1000,
                      nburnin = 100,
                      thin = 1)
